name: Tiffany Blue
lede: Tiffany Blue is a trademarked light turquoise tied to one jeweller; the name is a brand's, so the swatch on a screen is only an approximation.

sections.title: A jeweller's color
sections.body:
Paterson defines Tiffany blue as the turquoise-blue colour adopted by Tiffany, the jewellers [1]. Westland writes that it was first used on the cover of the firm's Blue Book in 1837, and that a custom Pantone shade for global use followed in 2001, made with the color company [2]. Eckstut gives a nearby but different account: the firm trademarked its signature color in 1998, and the custom Pantone number, 1837, honors the year the company was founded [3].

The two accounts overlap rather than clash: both tie the color to 1837 and to Pantone, while Westland dates the standardized color to 2001 and Eckstut dates the trademark to 1998, so they describe different events [2][3]. Westland says 1837 marks the Blue Book cover; Eckstut says it marks the founding year [2][3]. Eckstut uses the case to show how a name makes a color easier to remember [3].

sections.title: The swatch is not the box
sections.body: Our swatch is a bright turquoise-green and is only an approximation of a trademarked color [4]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 would call it a brilliant bluish green, about six units away, and the xkcd survey of 2010 gives a much paler aqua [4]. Printed boxes, lit rooms and screens each shift the color, so treat any hex as a pointer. Related names are [[turquoise]], [[robin-s-egg-blue]] and [[aqua]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 holds this color across even one per cent of the canvas, as photographed [4]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and it fits a color tied to a modern brand [4].

origin.source: Westland, Principles of Color; Eckstut, What Is Color?

questions.q: What does the Pantone number 1837 mark, by Eckstut's account?
choices: The year the company was founded
questions.answer: The year the company was founded

questions.q: True or false: the books read agree on one year of standardization.

openers: Compare Tiffany blue to a robin's egg: both are turquoise, but only one has a trademark.

issues: 'books disagree' reframed: 2001 standardization and 1998 trademark are different events, not a contradiction
